before: What shall we say then? That the more valuable things by nature have obtained the first mention; and then, that to one who examines carefully, all things will appear either to use seed or to have what is equivalent to seed. For poplars, and willows, and elms, and white poplars, and all such trees seem to bear no fruit from what is evident, but one who examines carefully would discover that each of these has seed. For the kernel under the leaf, which some of those who have occupied themselves with word-making call 'mischos,' has the power of seed. For whatever naturally comes to be from branches, for the most part puts forth roots from this. And perhaps the offshoots of the roots also hold the place of seed, which the gardeners pull off and increase the kind. But first, as we said, the things more essential to our life were deemed worthy of mention, all that were going to receive man with their own fruits and prepare for him an abundant way of life: the vine producing wine that was going to gladden the heart of man, and the olive providing fruit able to make the face cheerful with oil (Psalm 103:15 (104:15)). How many things came together at the same time, brought forth urgently by nature? The root of the vine; the branches around it, flourishing and great, spread above the ground; the shoot, the tendrils, the unripe grape, the clusters. A vine seen with understanding is enough for your sight to produce in you a reminder of nature. For you remember clearly the image of the Lord, that he calls himself the vine, and the Father the vinedresser, and he called each one of us, having been grafted into the Church through faith, branches (John 15:1-2). And he summons us to abundant fruit, so that we may not be condemned for uselessness and handed over to the fire. And he does not cease everywhere to compare the souls of men to vines. For a vineyard was made for the beloved, he says, on a horn, in a rich place (Isaiah 5:1). And, I planted a vineyard, and put a hedge around it (Isaiah 5:2). He clearly means the human souls as the vineyard, around which he put a hedge—the security from the commandments and the guard of the angels. For the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him (Psalm 33:8 (34:7)). Then he also fixed stakes for us, as it were, placing in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers (1 Corinthians 12:28). And by the examples of the ancient and blessed men he leads our thoughts to the height, and did not leave them thrown on the ground and worthy of being trampled. He also wants us to hold fast to our neighbors by the twining of love, as if by tendrils, and to rest upon them, so that always having our impulse toward what is above, like some climbing vines we may set ourselves beside the tops of the highest things. He also requires us to accept being dug around. And the soul is dug around in the putting away of the cares of the world, which are a weight on our hearts. So the one who has put away fleshly love, and the friendship toward money, or has considered the anxiety for this wretched little glory to be spit upon and contemptible, has been dug around, as it were, and has breathed again, having put off the vain weight of the earthly mind. But it is necessary, according to the word of the proverb, not to grow wild like wood—that is, not to live ostentatiously, nor to hunt for praise from outsiders—but to be fruitful, storing up the display of works for the true vinedresser.

before: And certainly whatever lies between these two also came into being together with the extremes. So even if Moses says nothing about the elements—fire, water, and air—you should understand by your own reasoning, first, that all things are mixed with all things. In earth you will find water, air, and fire: fire leaps out from stones, and from iron—which itself has its origin from the earth—abundant fire is wont to flash forth in friction. This is worth marveling at: fire exists within bodies and lurks there without harm, but once it is called outside, it is destructive of those guarding it for a time. Well-diggers show that the nature of water is present in the earth, and the vapors rising from earth moistened and warmed by the sun show the presence of air. Then further, if heaven by nature occupies the upper region and the earth is the lowest—because light things are carried toward heaven, while heavy things naturally sink down toward the earth, and up and down are most opposite to each other—then the one who mentioned the things most distant from each other by nature also indicated by synecdoche the things that fill the space between them. So do not seek an explanation of each individual thing, but understand what was passed over in silence through what was spoken.

“In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” The investigation of the substance of each existing thing—whether of those that fall under our contemplation or of those set before our senses—would introduce a long and detached discourse into the exposition, so that more words would be consumed in examining this problem than all the rest that can be said about each of the questions. And this would be of no benefit for the building up of the Church. But concerning the substance of heaven, we are satisfied with what Isaiah said. In simple words he gave us an adequate understanding of its nature when he said, “He who made firm the heaven as smoke” (Isaiah 40:22)—that is, he gave the heaven a fine nature for its composition, not a solid nor thick one. And concerning its shape, what he said is sufficient for us, when he said in praise of God, “He who set the heaven as a vault” (Isaiah 40:22). Let us give ourselves the same counsel concerning the earth: not to busy ourselves overmuch with its substance, whatever it may be, nor to wear ourselves out with reasonings by seeking out the underlying reality itself, nor to seek some nature devoid of qualities, existing without quality by its own definition. Rather, we should know well that everything observed about the earth is ordered toward the principle of its being, and these things complete its substance. For you will arrive at nothing if you try by reasoning to strip away each of the qualities that exist in it. If you remove the black, the cold, the heavy, the dense, the qualities of taste that exist in it, or any others that are observed about it, there will be no underlying reality left. So I urge you to leave these questions aside, and not to seek on what the earth stands. For the mind will grow dizzy this way too, as the reasoning proceeds toward no agreed-upon end.
